question: to the Commission Stefano Cavedagna (ECR) Subject:

Directive (EU) 2024/8251, which will apply from 27 September 2026, aims to combat greenwashing and provide consumers with accurate sustainability information. However, under the Commission’s current interpretation, businesses may be required to relabel, repackage or discard products already placed on the market that were compliant with the rules in force at the time of production. In sectors such as food and fast-moving consumer goods, this could generate significant food and packaging waste, contrary to the objectives of the Waste Framework Directive and the EU’s broader circular economy commitments, particularly given that the Commission only published its FAQs in November 2025. In this context: 1.
What measures is the Commission taking to prevent unnecessary food and packaging waste resulting from the application of the ECGT requirements to legacy stock already placed on the market?

How does the Commission intend to ensure that the implementation of the ECGT does not discourage food manufacturers from investing in sustainability initiatives while allowing them to continue communicating genuine sustainability commitments to consumers?

Directive (EU) 2024/825 of 28 February 2024 amending Directives 2005/29/EC and 2011/83/EU as regards empowering consumers for the green transition through better protection against unfair practices and through better information (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/825/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission endeavours to ensure that the application of Directive (EU) 2024/825 will not lead to unnecessary food or packaging waste. Under Regulation (EU) 2025/401, Member States shall reduce packaging waste generated per capita by 5% by 2030, 10% by 2035, and 15% by 2040, compared with 2018 levels. The Commission has published a Question & Answers document reflecting the main questions raised by traders and other stakeholders, including on ‘old stock’ situations. This document is a support tool and does not replace the traders’ own responsibility to prepare for the rules adopted in early 2024. The Commission remains in regular contact with stakeholders at EU and national level as well as national authorities to support a coherent application across the EU. In addition, the Commission facilitated exchanges within the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network concerning such ‘old stock’ situations. The CPC authorities have published a Common Understanding on the matter of old stock to support a coherent and proportionate enforcement approach across the EU. According to that CPC document, national authorities plan to take into account genuine transitional difficulties and practical constraints concerning old stock situations in their enforcement actions2. The Directive does not prevent food business operators from communicating genuine sustainability efforts. Businesses are encouraged to continue to communicate about their sustainability efforts, provided they are clear, accurate and not misleading. The new rules should strengthen consumer trust and support a level playing field for businesses.
